title: Values and borrowing in Rust
summary: Use a borrowed slice, a loop, and a condition to count positive values.

scenario.briefing: A robotics controller stores sensor changes in a vector. Count positive changes without taking ownership of the data.

objectives.description: Apply the taught syntax in a working file.

hints: The loop yields a reference to each value.

misconceptions.description: Assuming a slice parameter copies the data.
misconceptions.feedback: A slice reference borrows the existing data. No copy occurs.
Indexing panics on an invalid index. Use get for an Option.

misconceptions.testDescription: The loop counts only positive values.
misconceptions.feedback: count += 0 never changes the count. Increment in the positive branch.

sections.title: Rust values and decisions
sections.body: Rust binds values with let: let count: i32 = 3;. A binding is immutable unless it is declared with let mut. String owns text, while &str borrows it. Option<T> models absence and Result<T, E> models failure. if and match select branches, and match must cover every case. A for loop borrows a collection by reference: for value in &values { ... }.

steps.title: Check the semantics

statements.label: A let binding is immutable unless it is declared with mut.
A shared reference prevents the owner from being dropped while it is alive.
Indexing a slice out of bounds returns None.

steps.explanation: Borrowing gives temporary access without transferring ownership. Out-of-bounds indexing panics; get returns an Option.
